_readme: Level 3 Tax Code Book leaves (LevelBookLeaves). They appear after the shared book's three sections in Office_Level3 only; Levels 1 and 2 keep their own books.

T06 (L3-33): Section 4 Costs and Purpose and Section 5 Count Once land before Bea's worksheet check grades anything; the worksheet hints name them. T07: Section 6 Taxable Income, Section 7 the annual individual table (2023 onwards) and Section 8 Base Plus Excess, with the separate Practice Design Studio example. Later tickets append corporate conditions, credit versus expense and checking a computation (CONTENT.md).

Each term is printed like the shared pages' values (readOnly: true, so it cannot be picked up) with its explanation underneath: one paragraph (blank-line separated) per value; keep those counts equal.
Leaves explain concepts. Never put a client's amounts, a placement, a reason to choose or a total here.
Simplified classroom rules for this bounded exercise, not legal advice; content-authority review is pending (TAX_AUTHORITY.md).
Fields starting with '_' are notes and are ignored by the game.

sections.heading: Section 4 – Costs and Purpose
sections.body:
Spent to earn this year's business income, for the work itself, and shown by a record. It is listed with the other allowable costs and reduces the income they helped earn.

Personal spending, such as a family celebration or a gift, never reduces business income, even with a receipt.

A receipt proves that a payment happened, not what it was for. Read the record, and ask the client when its purpose is unclear, before deciding.

sections.heading: Section 5 – Count Once
sections.body:
One payment can appear on several papers: a summary row, the supplier's bill, a draft list. It is still one cost, counted once.

A bill or agreement that backs up a row already counted. Keep it with the worksheet as support, but do not add it again.

Papers that share a reference number, such as an order or invoice number, usually describe the same transaction. Compare them before adding anything.

Add exactly the entries in one section, each once, using the amounts from their records. When an entry moves in or out, the old subtotal is out of date: work it out again.

sections.heading: Section 6 – Taxable Income
sections.body:
All the income the year's records support, before anything is taken away.

The costs the records support for earning that income (Sections 4 and 5).

Gross income minus allowable expenses. This is the amount the rate table is applied to; it is not the tax.

sections.heading: Section 7 – Annual Individual Table (2023 onwards)
sections.body:
No tax.

15% of the excess over 250,000.

22,500 plus 20% of the excess over 400,000.

102,500 plus 25% of the excess over 800,000.

402,500 plus 30% of the excess over 2,000,000.

2,202,500 plus 35% of the excess over 8,000,000.

Annual taxable income, for a whole year. Find the one row whose range holds the amount: each row starts just above the one before it and includes its own top figure.

sections.heading: Section 8 – Base Plus Excess
sections.body:
The row's floor is where its range starts. Taxable income minus the floor is the excess.

Only the excess is multiplied by the row's rate; the income below the floor is already covered by the base tax.

Tax due is the row's base tax plus the tax on the excess. Keep every step on a tape, and round only the finished tax due to cents.

Practice Design Studio (not a client) has taxable income of 350,000: its row starts at 250,000, so the excess is 100,000, and 15% of it is 15,000 tax due (that row has no base tax).

sections.heading: Section 9 – Credit Versus Expense
sections.body:
An expense is a cost of earning income: allowable expenses come off gross income before the tax is worked out.

Tax withheld is different. When a payer withholds part of a payment, it pays that much of the payee's tax for them, and gives a certificate showing the payer, the payee, the period, the income payment and the tax withheld.

That tax is a credit. It comes off the tax due at the very end: tax due − credits = remaining payable. It is never another expense, and the income payment on the certificate is already in the payee's income records: count it once.

Use the certificate's tax withheld, for the same payee and the same tax year. Practice Design Studio (not a client) owes 15,000 tax due and holds a certificate for 2,000 withheld: 15,000 − 2,000 = 13,000 still to pay. More credits than tax due leave a balance below zero: keep its sign.

sections.heading: Section 10 – Checking a Computation
sections.body:
Check a computation in order: its sources and totals, taxable income, the rate row, tax due, then credits and the remaining payable. When one line is wrong, the lines built on it follow it: fix the first one, then recalculate what depends on it.

Ready for computation review means every line is supported and current. It is a recommendation to the Auditor, not filing a return or paying tax.

Not Ready is an honest hold: use it while a line is still open. Holding a fully supported computation, or stamping Ready over an open line, sends it back.

A stamp covers the sheet as it was when you stamped it. Any change afterwards makes it out of date: stamp the current sheet again before you hand it in.
